fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is a question I spent a lot of time thinking about, because when ViT and then Swin came out, the dominant narrative was that attention was fundamentally better than convolution for vision. And I was a bit skeptical of that, not because I had anything against transformers, but because I noticed that the comparisons were not really apples to apples. People were comparing a Swin Transformer trained with a very modern recipe against a ResNet-50 trained with a recipe from 2015. So the first thing we did in the ConvNeXt project was just retrain the ResNet with the same training procedure that the vision transformer papers were using: AdamW, a much longer schedule, Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, stochastic depth, label smoothing, all of that. And just that step moved ResNet-50 from around 76 percent to around 78.8 on ImageNet. So a decent chunk of the gap was never about architecture at all. It was about training.

After that, we did something fairly systematic. We took the ResNet and, one step at a time, asked whether a design decision that transformers made could be translated back into a convolutional network. Some of these are macro-level. The stage compute ratio in Swin is roughly one to one to three to one, so we changed the ResNet block distribution to match. ViT uses a patchify stem, a non-overlapping stride-four convolution, so we did that too. Then we borrowed the idea of depthwise convolution, which is actually very similar in spirit to the weighted sum within self-attention, in that it mixes information spatially but not across channels. We used an inverted bottleneck like in transformer MLP blocks, and we moved to larger kernels, seven by seven, because the whole appeal of attention is the large receptive field and modern convnets had converged on three by three for mostly historical reasons. And then there's a bunch of micro design: replacing ReLU with GELU, using fewer activation functions and fewer normalization layers, swapping BatchNorm for LayerNorm, adding separate downsampling layers.

Each one of these steps individually is small, sometimes a few tenths of a percent, but when you add them up you get a pure convolutional network that matches or beats Swin at the same compute on ImageNet, and also on COCO detection and ADE20K segmentation, which is where people thought the inductive biases of attention mattered most.

So how do I understand the gap? My honest take is that most of the measured gap at that time was the result of a slow accumulation of good engineering decisions in the transformer community that nobody had bothered to port back. It wasn't evidence that the operation itself, attention versus convolution, was the decisive factor. I'd say convolution and attention are both reasonable token mixers, and the macro structure, the normalization, the training recipe, and the scale of the data end up mattering at least as much.

That said, I don't want to overclaim. There are things transformers genuinely do better. They're far more natural when you want a single architecture across modalities, when you want to mix text and image tokens, or when you want flexible, variable-length inputs. At very large scale with multimodal pretraining the field has largely converged on transformers for good reasons. ConvNeXt was never meant to argue convnets are superior. It was meant to argue that we should be careful about what we attribute to architecture, and to set a fairer baseline so the question of convolution versus attention can actually be studied cleanly.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes retraining under the same recipe and systematically translating transformer design choices into a ConvNet one at a time to compare convolution and attention fairly.

r002.rationale: It directly attributes most of the measured gap to training recipes and accumulated architectural engineering choices, stating that attention itself was not the decisive factor.

opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the context matters a lot here. Around 2020 and 2021, Vision Transformers came out, then Swin Transformer, and they were beating ResNets on ImageNet and especially on downstream tasks like detection and segmentation. The narrative that formed pretty quickly was that attention is just better, and that the inductive biases of convolution, locality and translation equivariance, were holding us back.

What bothered me was that the comparisons weren't really apples to apples. The ResNet everyone used as a baseline was basically from 2015. It was trained with a 2015-era recipe: SGD, around 90 epochs, fairly light augmentation. The transformers came with a whole package of newer things: AdamW, much longer training, heavy augmentation like Mixup, CutMix, and RandAugment, stochastic depth, label smoothing. They also had a bunch of architectural design choices that had nothing to do with attention itself. So the question we asked was: how much of the gap is actually attention, and how much is everything else?

So we did something quite simple. We started from a standard ResNet-50 and modernized it step by step, borrowing ideas from the transformer side, while keeping it a pure ConvNet. No attention anywhere. We tracked accuracy at each step.

The first surprise was the training recipe alone. Just training ResNet-50 the way people trained DeiT or Swin took it from about 76 to almost 79 percent top-1. That's a big chunk of the "gap," with zero architectural change.

Then we went through the architecture:

- **Macro design.** We changed the stage compute ratio to match Swin and replaced the ResNet stem with a "patchify" stem, a 4×4 non-overlapping convolution with stride 4.
- **Depthwise convolutions.** We used depthwise convolutions, the ResNeXt idea, which is really analogous to the per-channel spatial mixing that self-attention does.
- **Block structure.** We used an inverted bottleneck like in the transformer MLP block, and larger kernels, 7×7, to get something closer to a larger window.
- **Micro design.** Many of these changes individually look almost trivial. We swapped ReLU for GELU, used fewer activation and normalization layers, switched BatchNorm to LayerNorm, and added separate downsampling layers.

At the end, you get ConvNeXt, and it matches or slightly beats Swin at comparable FLOPs on ImageNet, COCO, and ADE20K. It's also simpler and quite efficient in practice.

So my takeaway was that much of the performance gap people attributed to self-attention was really about training procedures and a collection of design decisions, many of which could be transplanted directly into a ConvNet. That doesn't mean transformers aren't great. They have real advantages, especially in how naturally they extend across modalities and how well they fit with things like masked modeling and multimodal training. But the specific claim that convolution is fundamentally inferior for vision didn't hold up once you controlled for everything else.

And more broadly, I think it's a lesson about how we do empirical research. When a new architecture wins, it's often winning as a package. It's worth pulling that package apart and asking which piece actually matters, because the answer is frequently not the piece that gets the headline.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes modernizing a ResNet step by step while keeping it a pure ConvNet with no attention, isolating the effects of training and architectural components from self-attention.

r002.rationale: It states that the performance gap was largely due to training procedures and architectural design choices, and concludes that convolution was not inherently inferior to self-attention for vision.

fable-5.text:
When we started that project, the question we asked ourselves was pretty simple: is the gap between ConvNets and vision transformers really about the attention mechanism, or is it about everything else that came along with transformers? Because when people compared, say, a Swin Transformer to a ResNet, they weren't just comparing two architectures — they were comparing architectures trained with completely different recipes, designed with very different levels of care, from different eras.

So what we did was take a standard ResNet-50 and gradually "modernize" it, step by step, toward the design choices that transformers had popularized. And the first thing we found was striking: just updating the training recipe alone — training longer, using AdamW, modern data augmentation like Mixup and CutMix, stochastic depth, label smoothing — took ResNet-50 from around 76% to over 78% on ImageNet. So a big chunk of the supposed gap was never architectural at all. It was the training procedure.

Then we went through the architecture itself: changing the stage compute ratio, using a patchify stem, adopting depthwise convolutions with wider channels, inverted bottlenecks, larger 7×7 kernels, and then smaller micro-design changes — GELU instead of ReLU, fewer activation and normalization layers, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm. Each step was a known technique, nothing exotic. But when you put them together, the resulting pure ConvNet — ConvNeXt — matched or exceeded Swin Transformers across ImageNet classification, COCO detection, and ADE20K segmentation, while keeping the simplicity and efficiency of standard convolutions.

So my understanding of the "gap" is that it was largely an artifact of comparing a 2015-era design philosophy against a 2021-era one. The inductive biases of convolution — locality, translation equivariance — are still very useful for vision. Attention isn't magic; a lot of what made transformers look better was the surrounding design and training choices, which turn out to be transferable. I think the broader lesson, which I keep coming back to in my research, is that we should be careful about attributing progress to the component that gets the headline. Often the quiet stuff — the recipe, the baselines — is doing more work than we give it credit for.

r001.rationale: The response describes progressively modernizing a ResNet and comparing the resulting ConvNeXt with Swin, but it does not clearly describe holding other architectural components constant to isolate convolution versus self-attention.

r002.rationale: It explicitly attributes the apparent gap largely to differing training recipes and architectural design eras, stating that convolution remains useful and that attention is not inherently superior.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, the starting point for that project was a kind of discomfort. Around 2021 the narrative had settled very quickly: transformers won, convolution was a legacy inductive bias, and the global receptive field of self-attention was the thing that explained the difference. And that story was plausible, but when I looked at the actual comparisons being made, they weren't clean. A Swin Transformer trained for 300 epochs with AdamW, Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, random erasing, stochastic depth, label smoothing — compared against a ResNet-50 number from 2016 trained for 90 epochs with SGD and basic augmentation. Those two numbers differ in the architecture, yes, but they also differ in almost everything else. So what was actually being measured?

So we took a very boring, almost mechanical approach. Start with a ResNet-50. Hold the compute roughly fixed. Change one thing at a time, in the direction of what the transformer papers were doing, and just write down the number after every step. First the training recipe alone — that gets you from 76.1 to 78.8 before you touch a single layer. Then the macro design: the stage compute ratio, replacing the stem with a patchify layer. Then depthwise convolution, the inverted bottleneck, moving the depthwise layer up, larger kernels. Then the micro stuff that feels almost cosmetic — GELU instead of ReLU, fewer activations, fewer norm layers, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, separate downsampling layers.

And at the end of that path you have ConvNeXt, and it matches or beats Swin on ImageNet, and on COCO and ADE20K too, with no attention anywhere in it.

Now, the conclusion I want to draw from that is narrower than how it sometimes gets quoted. I don't think we showed convnets are better than transformers. What we showed is that the evidence for the gap was substantially weaker than people believed, because the comparison was confounded. A lot of what we attribute to architecture is actually training procedure, scale, and the accumulated engineering effort that flows toward whatever is currently fashionable. Transformers still have real advantages — they're a more natural fit for multimodal data, for scaling to enormous datasets, for having one architecture across modalities. Those are genuine. But "self-attention sees globally, therefore it wins on ImageNet" — that specific claim didn't survive a controlled experiment. And I think that pattern repeats more often in our field than we'd like to admit.

r001.rationale: The response describes holding compute roughly fixed and changing one architectural or training component at a time, thereby addressing confounds and isolating what drives the ConvNet–transformer comparison.

r002.rationale: It argues that the apparent gap reflected confounding from design choices, training procedure, scale, and engineering rather than an inherent convolutional disadvantage, noting that a modernized ConvNet matched or beat Swin.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think much of the gap came from things other than convolution versus attention. When ViT came out, and later Swin Transformer, they were compared against ResNets, which were five or six years old by then. The ResNets were mostly trained with the older recipe: fewer epochs, SGD, light augmentation. The transformers were trained with modern recipes, meaning AdamW, long schedules, heavy augmentation like Mixup, CutMix and RandAugment, stochastic depth, and label smoothing. So the comparison mixed together two things, the architecture and everything around it.

In the paper we did a kind of controlled walk. We started with a plain ResNet-50 and first changed only the training recipe. That alone gave a surprisingly large improvement, from about 76 to nearly 79 on ImageNet, without touching the architecture. Then we moved step by step toward a Swin-like design while keeping it a pure convolutional network. We changed the stage compute ratio and used a patchify stem. We used depthwise convolution with a wider network, an inverted bottleneck, and larger kernels, around 7x7. On the smaller details, we used GELU instead of ReLU, fewer activation and normalization layers, and LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm. Each step helped a bit, and the end result, ConvNeXt, matched or slightly beat Swin at similar FLOPs on ImageNet classification, COCO detection, and ADE20K segmentation.

What I take from that is that there wasn't a big intrinsic advantage of self-attention for standard vision tasks. A lot of what looked like a Transformer advantage was really a combination of training recipes and macro design choices, such as hierarchical stages, large receptive fields, and the block structure. Many of these could be borrowed into a ConvNet. It's also telling that Swin itself reintroduced locality and hierarchy, which are very convolutional ideas. That suggests those priors still matter in vision.

I don't want to overstate it, though. I'm not saying Transformers don't matter. They have real practical advantages. They're flexible across modalities, they share an architecture with language models, and the tooling and scaling infrastructure around them is excellent. Those are good reasons to use them, but they're different from saying the convolution itself is the limitation. The main lesson for me was to be careful about attributing a performance gain to a headline architectural idea when many other things changed at the same time.

r001.rationale: The response describes a controlled, step-by-step progression from ResNet toward a Swin-like design while keeping the model purely convolutional and varying specific design components to isolate their effects.

r002.rationale: It explicitly attributes the apparent Transformer advantage to training recipes and macro-design choices, stating there was no large intrinsic advantage of self-attention over convolution for standard vision tasks.

haiku-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the gap was much less about attention itself than people assumed. The common story was that vision transformers were fundamentally better at vision and convnets had hit a ceiling. But when you compare a vanilla ResNet with a Swin transformer, many of the differences are in training recipes, like AdamW, longer schedules, heavy augmentation such as Mixup and CutMix, and stochastic depth, and in macro design, like how the network is staged, how the input is patchified, and where normalization and activations go.

So we started from a ResNet-50 and modernized it step by step, tracking what each change bought us. The architectural changes were fairly modest: a 4x4 non-overlapping patchify stem, depthwise convolutions, an inverted bottleneck, and larger kernels, which we settled at 7x7. We also used fewer activation and normalization layers, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, and separate downsampling layers. None of these is exotic on its own. The end result was a pure ConvNet that matched Swin on ImageNet classification and performed comparably on COCO detection and ADE20K segmentation.

What I find most interesting is the 7x7 kernel, because it weakens part of the "attention is special" argument. People emphasized the global receptive field, but large depthwise convolutions give you a big receptive field too, while keeping a local inductive bias that still helps. So I don't think the lesson is that convolutions beat transformers. It's that a lot of what we credited to the architecture family was really about the design choices around it, and when you hold those fixed, the two look much closer than the headlines suggested.

I'd add a caveat, though. Our results were mostly on the benchmarks people were already using, and scale and data regimes matter a lot. So I'd be careful about reading it as a clean win for ConvNets. The performance gap was never as fundamental, or as architecture-driven, as it was sometimes presented.

r001.rationale: The response describes modernizing a ResNet step by step while tracking each change, and comparing models with training recipes and macro-architectural choices controlled, to assess the convolution-versus-attention difference.

r002.rationale: It explicitly argues that the gap was driven largely by training and architectural design choices, not by an inherent inferiority of convolution, and says the models look much closer when those factors are held fixed.

astra-6.text:
The question we wanted to ask was: how much of that gap actually comes from self-attention, and how much comes from all the other things that changed along with vision transformers? When you compare a modern transformer with a traditional ResNet, you’re also comparing different training recipes and different architectural design choices. So it’s difficult to attribute the improvement to just one component.

In “A ConvNet for the 2020s,” we started with a conventional convolutional network and gradually modernized it, taking inspiration from the design of vision transformers while keeping the network convolutional. That led to ConvNeXt, which could compete very strongly with transformers.

For me, the takeaway is that the earlier comparisons understated what convolution could do. Attention is useful, but those results didn’t establish that it was necessary for strong performance on these vision tasks. A lot depended on how you designed and trained the whole system. And I think that’s a useful lesson more broadly: when a new architecture becomes popular, we should also revisit the older alternatives with the same care and modern tools.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: how much of that gap comes from self-attention itself, and how much comes from everything else that changed along with vision transformers? When we compare a modern transformer with a convolutional network designed years earlier, we’re also comparing different training recipes and different architectural choices. So it’s difficult to attribute the improvement to attention alone.

In “A ConvNet for the 2020s,” we tried to disentangle those factors. We started with a standard ResNet and modernized it step by step, taking inspiration from the design of hierarchical vision transformers while keeping convolution as the core operation. That process led to ConvNeXt, which could compete with strong vision transformers in both accuracy and efficiency.

For me, the takeaway is that convolution was still a very competitive building block. Some of the apparent gap reflected how much effort had gone into developing the surrounding architecture and training procedure. That doesn’t mean attention has no advantages. It means that, to understand those advantages, we need strong baselines where the other ingredients are comparable.

luna-5.6.text:
I think the gap was real in the benchmarks, but it was easy to misinterpret what it meant. It wasn’t necessarily that self-attention was fundamentally superior to convolution. A lot of the advantage came from the fact that vision transformers introduced a newer generation of design choices and training practices, while convolutional networks were often represented by an older ResNet recipe.

In ConvNeXt, we tried to modernize the convolutional network step by step: using larger kernels, depthwise convolutions, an inverted bottleneck, fewer activation and normalization layers, LayerNorm, and the same stronger training recipe used for transformers. Once we made that controlled comparison, a pure convolutional model could match or outperform models like Swin Transformer, while remaining simpler and often more efficient. So my takeaway is that the apparent performance gap was largely a gap in model design and training technology, rather than proof that convolution had become obsolete. Transformers are very powerful and flexible, but convolution still provides useful locality, translation structure, and computational efficiency.

So the work suggests that many of the gains attributed to transformers came from good design and training choices that ConvNets could adopt too.
